title: Growing up: how a body grows from baby to grown-up, and how we measure growing

summary.text: Are you taller when you wake up than when you go to bed? A newborn baby is about 50 centimetres long. By the age of 7, most children are more than twice as tall. Children grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year, and stop getting taller in their teens. Your child marks their height on the wall at bedtime and again in the morning, and finds that height changes in a single night.
summary.art: A strip of paper taped to a door frame with a blue pencil line and a slightly higher red line, a hardback book and a ruler beside it, and a girl in a nightdress standing against the frame.

intro.hook: Are you the same height at bedtime as when you wake up in the morning?
intro.text: Find a shirt or frock you wore three years ago. Try it on. The sleeves stop above your wrists, and it feels tight. You grew, but you never saw yourself growing. Growing happens too slowly to watch. So people measure, and write the numbers down. In this unit you learn how a body grows from a baby to a grown-up. You also learn to measure yourself carefully. Then you test a strange idea: that you are taller in the morning.
intro.art: A girl of 7 trying on a small frock from when she was 4, with the sleeves far above her wrists, laughing in front of a mirror.

outcomes: By the end I can name the stages of a human life, from baby to older adult, and say how a body changes in each.
By the end I can measure my height carefully, with a book, a mark on paper and a ruler, the same way each time.
By the end I can say that children grow a few centimetres each year, fastest as babies, and stop getting taller in their teens.
By the end I can explain why people are a little taller in the morning than at bedtime.
By the end I can say what helps a body grow: food, sleep, being healthy, care, and what we get from our parents.
By the end I can compare two measurements, say which is bigger and by how much, and spot a pattern.

terms.meaning: To grow is to get bigger and change as time passes.
terms.example: A baby grows into a child. Your feet grow, so old chappals stop fitting.
terms.art: A row of three chappals from small to big, next to a child's bare foot.

terms.meaning: Your height is how tall you are, from the floor to the top of your head.
terms.example: A child of 7 may be 120 centimetres tall. A grandmother may be 150 centimetres tall.
terms.art: A girl standing straight against a wall, with an arrow from the floor to the top of her head.

terms.meaning: A centimetre is a small, fixed length we use to measure. It is about as wide as your little fingernail.
terms.example: A school ruler is 15 or 30 centimetres long. Each centimetre has ten tiny lines, called millimetres.
terms.art: A school ruler with one centimetre shown large, and ten tiny millimetre lines inside it.

terms.meaning: An adult is a person, or another animal, who has finished growing up.
terms.example: Your parents, aunts and grandparents are adults. Adults stop getting taller.
terms.art: A grandmother, a mother and a father standing together.

terms.meaning: A life stage is one part of a life: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult or older adult.
terms.example: You are in the child stage. A grandparent may be in the older adult stage.
terms.art: Six people in a row from a baby lying down to a grandmother with a walking stick.

terms.meaning: Your backbone is a column of small bones down your back. Between the bones are soft pads called discs.
terms.example: Run a finger down a grown-up's back and feel the bumps. Each bump is one bone of the backbone.
terms.art: A drawing of a backbone: a stack of small bones with soft round pads between them, like a stack of idlis with cushions between.

terms.meaning: A growth spurt is a time when a person grows much faster than usual.
terms.example: Most teenagers have a growth spurt. A girl may grow 8 centimetres in one year.
terms.art: A teenage girl standing next to last year's height mark, which is now at her nose.

explanations.concept: Growing up means getting bigger and changing
explanations.context: This card is about what changes in a human body from birth to old age.
explanations.definition: Growing up is how a baby's body gets bigger and changes, until they become an adult.
explanations.description: Every person goes through the same life stages: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult and older adult. A newborn cannot sit or walk and drinks only milk. A toddler walks and talks. A child loses milk teeth, and adult teeth grow in. Adults stop getting taller, but their bodies keep changing, and some older people become a little shorter.
examples: A baby gets their first tooth at about 6 months.
Milk teeth start to fall out at about 6 or 7 years.
By about age 6, a child's brain is nearly as big as a grown-up's.
Many grandparents are a little shorter than they were at 30.
explanations.art: A row of human stages: a baby lying on a mat, a toddler walking, a girl of 7, a teenage girl, a mother and a grandmother.

explanations.context: This card is about how much a child grows each year, and when growing stops.
explanations.definition: Babies grow fastest. Children then grow slowly and steadily, teenagers have a growth spurt, and then growing taller stops.
explanations.description: A newborn baby is about 50 centimetres long. In the first year a baby grows about 25 centimetres, which is the fastest anyone grows after birth. After the age of 2, children grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year. That is about a millimetre a week, too slow to see. In the teens there is a growth spurt, and then growing taller stops: at about 15 or 16 for most girls and 17 or 18 for most boys.
examples: Seven years old: often about 115 to 125 centimetres.
A grown-up woman in India is often about 150 to 160 centimetres.
explanations.art: A bar chart drawn as children standing in a row by age, 0 to 18, getting taller quickly at first, then slowly, then quickly again in the teens, then staying the same.

explanations.concept: Why you are taller in the morning
explanations.context: This card is about the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment, where you marked your height at bedtime and again in the morning.
explanations.definition: Most people are a little taller in the morning, because the soft discs in their backbone are squashed during the day and fill up again during sleep.
explanations.description: Your backbone is a stack of small bones with a soft disc between each pair. The discs hold water, a bit like a wet sponge. When you stand and walk, your weight squashes the discs and presses some water out, so they get thinner. At night you lie flat and the weight is off, so the discs soak water back up. That is why you are a little taller when you wake up. Children lose about half a centimetre to one and a half centimetres in a day, mostly in the first few hours after getting up.
examples: Astronauts in space grow a few centimetres taller, because nothing presses their discs together. They shrink back on Earth.
Doctors try to measure a child at the same time of day each visit, so the change does not fool them.
explanations.art: Two side views of a backbone: in the evening the soft discs between the bones are thin and flat, and in the morning they are thick and round.

explanations.context: This card is about why some children grow taller than others.
explanations.definition: Growing needs good food, enough sleep, good health and care. How tall a person ends up also depends on what they get from their parents.
explanations.description: A body builds new bone and muscle out of food. Milk, dal, eggs, fish, ragi and green leaves all help. In deep sleep the body makes more growth hormone, a chemical message that tells bones to grow. Long illness, like diarrhoea again and again, slows growing down. Children also get some of their height from their parents. Scientists agree that all of these matter. They argue about how much each one matters.
examples: Children in many countries are taller today than 100 years ago, mainly because of better food and health.
Identical twins usually grow to almost the same height.

perspectives.explanation: When children have enough food and good health, most of the difference in height between people comes from what they get from their parents.

perspectives.who: Many child health scientists, such as the team behind the WHO growth study
perspectives.explanation: Healthy, well-fed babies in very different countries grow almost the same. So when many children in one place are short, the main reason is food, illness and dirty water, not their families.

explanations.art: A plate of rice, sambar, a boiled egg and greens, a child sleeping, and a mother and daughter standing back to back to compare height.

explanations.concept: Smooth or in jumps: how do babies grow?
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: does a child grow a tiny bit every day?
explanations.definition: Some scientists found that babies grow in sudden jumps, with long gaps in between. Others think most growing is smooth and steady.
explanations.description: Most growth charts draw a smooth curve. In 1992, Michelle Lampl, an American scientist, measured babies very often, some of them every day. She found that a baby often did not grow at all for days or weeks, and then grew between half a centimetre and two and a half centimetres all at once. Other scientists said small measuring mistakes could make smooth growth look like jumps. The argument is not settled.
examples: A baby's length stays the same for 10 days, then jumps by 1 centimetre.
A child's height measured once a year looks like a smooth line, because the jumps are hidden.

perspectives.explanation: Babies grow in jumps. Between the jumps there are long gaps with no growth at all.
Measuring a wriggling baby is hard. Small mistakes add up, so growth may really be smoother than it looks.

explanations.art: Two lines on a chart side by side: one smooth curve going up, and one staircase line going up in sudden steps.

agreed.text: Every human goes through the same life stages: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult and older adult. Humans and other animals all grow from young into adults.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have measured millions of children all over the world. Every healthy child grows in the same order of changes.

agreed.text: Children grow fastest in their first year, then about 5 to 6 centimetres a year, then fast again in the teens. Growing taller stops in the late teens.
agreed.evidence: Growth charts made from measuring many thousands of children, such as the WHO charts of 2006, all show this pattern.

agreed.text: People are a little taller in the morning than in the evening.
agreed.evidence: A doctor in England wrote about it about 300 years ago. Many studies since then have measured adults and children through the day, and found children lose about half a centimetre to one and a half centimetres.

challenging.claim: Children in some countries are just naturally smaller, so they need their own growth charts.
challenging.who: A common idea, held by many doctors until the 1990s
challenging.for: Children in different countries were often different heights on average. Adults in different places are different heights too.
challenging.against: The WHO study of 1997 to 2003 followed healthy, well-fed babies in Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and the United States. Babies in all six grew almost the same.
challenging.context: This card is about whether babies in India grow differently from babies elsewhere.

challenging.claim: Children grow in sudden jumps, not a little every day.
challenging.for: When she measured babies very often, many did not grow for days, then grew up to 2 and a half centimetres at once.
challenging.against: Other scientists say small measuring mistakes can look like jumps. Measuring a moving baby is hard.
challenging.context: This card is about how growing happens day by day.

challenging.claim: Children grow faster in some seasons than in others.
challenging.who: Rasmus Malling-Hansen, who measured children at a school in Denmark in the 1880s, and later scientists
challenging.for: He measured the same children very often for years, and found faster growth in height at some times of year.
challenging.against: Other studies found only small or mixed season effects. Nobody knows for sure why there would be one.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the time of year changes how fast children grow.

big_questions.q: Almost every part of your body has grown and changed since you were a baby. So what makes you still you?
big_questions.hint: Your size changed, your teeth changed and your hair changed. Your name and your memories stayed. Is that what makes you you?

big_questions.q: If your height is different in the morning and at night, what is your real height?
big_questions.hint: In the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment, your morning mark was higher than your bedtime mark. Is one of the marks wrong? Or are both true?

big_questions.q: You did not see yourself grow even one day. How do you know you grew at all?
big_questions.hint: Think of old clothes, old chappals and marks on the wall. What do they show?

big_questions.q: The food you ate last week is now part of your bones. Where does the food end and where do you begin?
big_questions.hint: Your bones are built from milk, dal, ragi and greens. Is it still food, or is it you?

big_questions.q: Why do humans take so many years to grow up, when a calf can walk on her first day?
big_questions.hint: Think about how much a child learns while growing up.

story.title: The Two Lines on the Kitchen Door
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that people are a little taller in the morning, and that this is because the discs in the backbone are squashed during the day.
text: Meenakshi lived on the third floor of a building in Mysuru. She was seven. She lived with her Amma, her little brother Arjun, who was three, and her grandmother, Ajji.

Inside the kitchen door, Ajji kept a secret. It was a row of pencil lines, one above the other. Next to each line was a name and a date. Every Ugadi morning, Ajji measured everyone in the family, and drew a new line.
This Ugadi, Meenakshi woke up early. The house smelled of mango leaves and jaggery. "Ajji, measure me first!" she said, still in her nightdress.

Ajji took a thick book from the shelf. "Stand straight. Heels on the floor, back on the door." She laid the book flat on Meenakshi's head, pressed it against the door, and drew a line under it. Then she took the long tailor's tape from her sewing tin.
"One hundred and twenty centimetres," said Ajji. "Last Ugadi you were one hundred and fourteen. You grew six centimetres this year."
Meenakshi looked at the gap between her two lines. It was as wide as three of her fingers. "But I never felt myself grow," she said.
"Nobody does," said Ajji. "Six centimetres in a whole year is only about a millimetre a week. It is far too slow to see. That is why we draw lines."
In the evening, Meenakshi's cousin Kavya came from Chennai for the festival. Kavya was nine, and she wanted to know who was taller. "Measure me, and then measure Meenakshi again," she said.
Ajji laughed and fetched the book. Kavya's line was high above. Then Meenakshi stood against the door. Ajji drew a light line under the book.
Meenakshi turned round and stared. The new line was below her morning line. Not by much, only the width of a grain of rice. But it was below.
"I am shrinking!" she cried. "I grew six centimetres, and now I am getting smaller!"
Arjun started to cry too, because his sister was crying.

Amma came in from the balcony. Amma was a nurse at the children's clinic near the market. She looked at the two lines and smiled. "You are not shrinking for ever," she said. "Let's test it. Everyone gets measured tonight, before bed. Then again tomorrow, as soon as we wake up."

So that night Ajji measured Kavya, Meenakshi, Amma, and even Ajji herself, with Amma drawing her line. They used a blue pencil. In the morning, before anyone walked about, they did it all again with a red pencil.
Every red line was higher than the blue line. Meenakshi's was higher by about half a centimetre. Amma's was higher by more than a centimetre.

"Feel my back," said Amma. Meenakshi ran her finger down Amma's back and felt the bumps. "Each bump is a small bone," said Amma. "Between the bones are soft pads, called discs. All day your weight presses down and squashes them a little. At night you lie down, and they fill up again, like a sponge in water."
"So I am taller in the morning," said Meenakshi slowly, "and shorter at night. Every day!"
"Every day," said Amma. "That is why at the clinic, we write down the time when we measure a child."

Meenakshi took the pencil and wrote a small word next to her Ugadi line: "morning". "Next Ugadi," she said, "I will be measured in the morning again. Then the lines will tell the truth about my growing."
Arjun had stopped crying. He stood against the door on his tiptoes. "Me too," he said. "Measure me in the morning, and I will be the tallest."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenakshi first thinks her height is one fixed number. The evening line shows her that height changes during each day. The family's test shows why, and why measuring at the same time of day matters when you want to see real growth.
ask: Why could Meenakshi not feel herself growing?
Why was Meenakshi's evening line below her morning line?
Why did the family measure everyone in the morning before anyone walked about?
When should Meenakshi be measured next Ugadi, and why?
art: Inside a kitchen door in a Mysuru flat, a grandmother pressing a thick book on a girl's head, with a row of dated pencil lines on the door and mango leaves over the doorway.
A girl staring at two close pencil lines on a door, the evening one just below the morning one, while her older cousin watches.
A family in nightclothes in the morning: a mother standing against the door while the grandmother draws a red line under a book.
A girl running her finger down her mother's back, feeling the bumps of the backbone.

experiments.title: Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall: are you taller when you wake up?
experiments.context: In this experiment you mark your height on a paper strip at bedtime. Next morning, as soon as you get up, you mark it again. A grown-up does the same. Then you compare the marks.
experiments.question: Are you the same height at bedtime and in the morning, or does your height change overnight?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Tomorrow morning, will you be taller, shorter or the same as at bedtime? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone is measured at the same spot on the same wall, barefoot, with hair clips and buns taken out. The same book is used each time. Each person is measured three times, because one try can be a little wrong. We measure a grown-up too, so we can compare a child's change with a grown-up's.

materials.item: two strips of paper, each about 30 centimetres long, cut from the edge of a newspaper or an old notebook page (one for your child, one for a grown-up)
cellotape or masking tape, to stick the strip on a wall or door frame
a hardback book, or a steel plate with a flat rim
a blue pencil or pen and a red one
a school ruler with millimetre lines

schedule.what: At bedtime: tape the strip on the wall, guess, then mark everyone's height three times in blue.
In the morning, as soon as you get up: mark everyone again in red. Then measure the gaps and talk about them.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Keep the paper strips with their blue and red lines.

setup.art: A strip of newspaper taped upright on a door frame, at the height of a child's head, with a hardback book, a blue and a red pencil, and a ruler on a stool beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a paper strip on the wall at head height.

setup.art: A barefoot girl standing straight against the strip, heels on the floor, while her mother holds a book flat on her head against the wall and draws a blue line under it.
setup.caption: 2. At bedtime, hold the book flat on the head and draw a blue line.

setup.art: The same girl in the morning, sleepy, standing against the strip while her mother draws a red line under the book.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, straight out of bed, draw a red line.

setup.art: A close-up of the paper strip with a blue line and a red line just above it, and a ruler held against them showing the small millimetre lines.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the gap between the lines with a ruler.

flow.do: Ask your child the question, and wait for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the strip.
flow.say: Tonight we will measure you. Tomorrow morning we will measure you again. Will you be taller, shorter or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. In the morning, will you be taller, shorter or the same? Why?

good: The same, because I do not grow in one night.
Taller, because I grow while I sleep.
Shorter, because I am tired in the morning.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine, as long as there is a reason. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Choose a wall or door frame with a flat floor in front of it. 2. Tape one paper strip upright, with its middle at your child's head height. Tape the second strip at the grown-up's head height. 3. Stick a piece of tape on the floor along the wall, where the heels will go.
flow.say: We must stand on the same spot every time. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Help tape the paper on the wall. Put a tape mark on the floor for your heels.
flow.parent: A door frame works well. If the floor tiles are uneven, use the same tile each time.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands barefoot with heels, bottom and shoulders touching the wall. 2. Take out hair clips and buns. 3. Hold the book flat on the head, pressed against the wall. 4. Draw a short blue line under the book. 5. Your child steps away and back. Repeat three times.
flow.say: Stand tall, look straight ahead, and keep your heels down. I will draw a line under the book. Now step away and come back, and we do it again.
flow.kid: Stand straight. Heels down. Look ahead. Keep still while the line is drawn. Do it three times.
flow.parent: The three lines are often a millimetre or two apart. Use the middle one. Then let your child help mark the grown-up in the same way, with a stool if needed. Write each name beside the lines.

flow.do: Next morning, before your child walks about, measure them again exactly the same way, three times, with the red pencil. Then measure the grown-up.
flow.say: Good morning! Straight to the wall, before you do anything else. Heels down, look ahead.
flow.kid: Go to the wall as soon as you get up. Stand straight. Three red lines.
flow.wait: Next morning, as soon as you get out of bed
flow.parent: Do this within about 10 minutes of getting up. Most of the height is lost in the first hours of the day.

flow.do: 1. Look at the blue and red lines for each person. 2. Put the ruler's zero on the middle blue line. 3. Count the tiny lines up to the middle red line. Each tiny line is one millimetre. 4. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Which line is higher, the blue one or the red one? Let's count the tiny lines between them. Each one is a millimetre.
flow.kid: Which line is higher? Count the tiny lines between them.

good: The grown-up changed more than me.

flow.parent: Usually the red morning line is higher, often by 4 to 10 millimetres for a child, and often more for a grown-up. If the lines are the same for your child, look at the grown-up's lines. Then try again tomorrow night, standing very still and pressing the book firmly.

flow.do: Ask your child what they think, what they saw, and why it happened.
flow.say: Was your guess right? You did not grow a whole centimetre in one night. So why was the morning line higher?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Why was the red line higher?

ask.q: Why was the morning line higher?
good: Something in me got squashed in the day and came back at night.
Lying down all night made me longer.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the lines: 'My red line was 6 millimetres higher than my blue line.' Now read the card on why you are taller in the morning.

check.q: You are measured at bedtime and again the next morning. What usually happens?
options: You are a little taller in the morning
You are a little taller at bedtime
You are always exactly the same
check.why: At night you lie flat, and the soft discs in your backbone fill up again. So you are a little taller in the morning. If you picked bedtime, look at your own blue and red lines again.

experiments.title: Arms Out: is your arm span the same as your height?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stretch your arms out wide and measure from one fingertip to the other with a string. That length is your arm span. Then you compare it with your height, for everyone at home.
experiments.question: Is a person's arm span the same as their height, longer, or shorter?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Is your arm span longer than your height, shorter, or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We measure everyone barefoot, against the same wall. Arms are stretched straight out at shoulder height, with fingers straight. We use the same string for every person, and cut each string in the same way.

materials.item: a ball of string, wool or thin rope
children's scissors
cellotape and small paper labels
a ruler or a tailor's tape, if you have one

schedule.what: Cut a height string and an arm span string for each person, then compare them.

experiments.record: Tape each person's two strings side by side on a sheet of paper or on the floor, with labels.

setup.art: A girl standing with her back to a wall, arms stretched out wide, while a grown-up holds a string from one fingertip to the other.
setup.caption: 1. Stretch your arms out wide. Measure fingertip to fingertip with string.

setup.art: The same girl standing straight while a string is held from the floor to the top of her head.
setup.caption: 2. Measure your height with another string.

setup.art: Two strings taped side by side on the floor, labelled 'height' and 'arm span', almost the same length.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the two strings side by side and compare.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Stretch your arms out wide. Is that longer than you are tall, or shorter, or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stretch your arms wide. Is that longer than you are tall? Why?

good: Longer, because my arms look long.
Shorter, because I am tall.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands with their back to the wall, arms straight out at shoulder height. 2. A grown-up holds the string end at one middle fingertip. 3. Stretch the string to the other middle fingertip and cut it. 4. Label it 'arm span'.
flow.say: Arms out straight, like an aeroplane. Fingers straight too. Keep still while we cut the string.
flow.kid: Arms out wide. Fingers straight. Keep still.
flow.parent: Two people make this easier: one holds each end of the string.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands barefoot against the wall. 2. Hold the string end on the floor at the heel. 3. Stretch it up to the top of the head, under a flat book. 4. Cut it and label it 'height'.
flow.say: Now stand straight. This string will be as long as you are tall.
flow.kid: Stand straight against the wall. Keep still.

flow.do: Measure everyone at home the same way. Tape each person's two strings side by side. Hold them together and see which is longer. If you have a tape, measure the difference in centimetres and write it in the table.
flow.say: Let's do everyone at home too. Whose two strings are closest to the same?
flow.kid: Measure everyone. Put their two strings side by side.

good: My two strings are almost the same.
A grown-up's arm span is a bit longer than their height.

flow.parent: For most people the two strings are close, within a few centimetres. Some people's arm span is a little longer, and some a little shorter. Both are normal.

flow.do: Talk about what you found.
flow.say: Was your guess right? Why do you think arm span and height are so close?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Are your two strings close?

check.q: You measure the arm span and the height of everyone in a family. What will you most likely find?
options: Arm span and height are close for most people
Arm span is always twice the height
Arm span is always much shorter than height
check.why: For most people, arm span and height are within a few centimetres of each other. Your own strings show this.

activities.title: Too Small Now: the old clothes test
activities.context: In this activity you try on clothes or chappals you wore a few years ago. You find out which parts of you grew the most.

materials.item: a shirt, frock, kurta or school uniform from 2 or 3 years ago, or old chappals
if none are kept, a younger cousin's clothes, or a photo of you at 3 or 4

schedule.what: Try on old clothes, see where they are too small, and talk about which parts grew.

activities.record: Tell a grown-up the places where the clothes were too small, and they write them down.

setup.art: A small old frock and a pair of tiny chappals laid out on a bed.
setup.caption: 1. Find clothes or chappals from a few years ago.

setup.art: A girl in a too-small frock with the sleeves far above her wrists and the hem above her knees, looking in a mirror.
setup.caption: 2. Try them on. Where are they too small?

flow.do: Show your child the old clothes. Ask when they wore them.
flow.say: You wore this a few years ago. Do you think it still fits? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at these old clothes. Do you think they still fit?

flow.do: Your child tries them on. Look together at the sleeves, the length, the waist and the chappal heels.
flow.say: Where is it too short? Where is it too tight? Show me with your finger.
flow.kid: Put them on. Where are they too short? Where are they tight?

ask.q: Which part of you grew the most?
good: My arms. The sleeves are short.
My legs. The frock is too short now.
My feet stick out of the chappals.

flow.parent: Most children find the sleeves and the length too short. Arms and legs grow a lot in childhood.

flow.do: Talk about it.
flow.say: You grew all this, but you never saw yourself grow. How did the clothes show it?
flow.kid: You did not see yourself grow. How did the clothes show it?

check.q: A girl of 7 tries on a frock she wore when she was 4. The sleeves stop above her wrists. What does this show?
options: The frock has shrunk in the wash
Her arms are the same, but her hands grew
check.why: The sleeves stop above her wrists because her arms grew longer. Clothes are a record of how big we were.

activities.title: Feet in a Row: is the oldest foot the biggest?
activities.context: In this activity you draw round the foot of everyone at home, cut the outlines out, and put them in order by size. Then you put them in order by age. Are the two orders the same?

materials.item: old newspaper or used paper
a pencil and children's scissors
a ruler

schedule.what: Draw round everyone's foot and cut the outlines out. Put them in order by size, then by age, and compare the two orders.

activities.record: Glue or tape the feet in a row on the floor or in your notebook, with names and ages.

setup.art: A bare foot standing on newspaper while a child draws round the foot with a pencil.

setup.caption: 2. Put the feet in order, smallest to biggest.

flow.do: 1. Each person stands barefoot on paper. 2. Your child draws round the foot. 3. Cut out each outline and write the name and age on it.
flow.say: Stand still while I draw round your foot. Now you draw round mine.
flow.kid: Draw round each person's foot. Cut it out. Write their name and age.

flow.do: Your child puts the feet in a row from smallest to biggest. Then your child measures each one with the ruler.
flow.say: Put the feet in a row, from the smallest to the biggest. How long is each one?
flow.kid: Line up the feet, smallest to biggest. Measure each one.

flow.say: Now let's line them up by age, youngest to oldest. Is it the same order?
flow.kid: Now line them up by age. Is it the same order?

ask.q: Is the oldest person's foot the biggest?
good: No, an older person's foot can be smaller than a younger person's.
Children's feet are in age order, but grown-ups are mixed up.

flow.parent: Children's feet usually line up in age order, because children are still growing. Grown-ups often do not, because they have stopped growing. A grandmother's foot can be smaller than her son's. If only two of you are at home, also draw round the foot of a cousin or neighbour, if you can, or just compare your child's foot with the grown-up's.

activities.title: As Heavy as a Newborn: the atta packet baby
activities.context: In this activity you hold a bundle as heavy as a newborn baby. Then you think about how much heavier you are now.

materials.item: three 1-kilogram packets of atta, rice, salt or sugar, or a kitchen scale and a bag of potatoes
a small towel or a cloth bag
a bathroom scale, if you have one

schedule.what: Wrap three 1-kilogram packets in a towel, hold the 'baby', and compare with your own weight.

activities.record: Write: 'A newborn is about 3 kilograms. I am about ___ kilograms.'

setup.art: Three packets of atta wrapped together in a small towel like a baby.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap three 1-kilogram packets in a towel.

setup.art: A girl holding the towel bundle carefully in both arms, supporting it like a baby.
setup.caption: 2. Hold your 'baby'. That is how heavy a newborn is.

flow.do: Wrap three 1-kilogram packets in the towel. Give the bundle to your child to hold.
flow.say: Most babies weigh about 3 kilograms when they are born. Hold this bundle. That is how heavy you were.
flow.kid: Hold the bundle. You were about this heavy when you were born.

flow.do: If you have a bathroom scale, weigh your child. If not, ask how many packets they think they weigh.
flow.say: How many packets do you think you weigh now? Let's check.
flow.kid: How many packets do you weigh now? Guess, then check.
flow.parent: Many 7-year-olds weigh about 18 to 25 kilograms, so about 6 to 8 times their birth weight. Every child is different. Do not compare children's weights in a way that hurts.

flow.do: Talk about it.
flow.say: Where did all that extra weight come from?
flow.kid: Where did all your extra weight come from?

good: From food and milk.
My body made it out of the food I ate.

activities.title: My Birth Numbers: ask the family
activities.context: In this activity you find out how long and how heavy you were when you were born. Then you compare those numbers with your size now.

materials.item: your health card or vaccination card, if the family has it, or a family member who remembers
a string and scissors

schedule.what: Ask the family your birth length and weight, cut a string that long, and compare with your height now.

activities.record: Tape your birth-length string on a sheet of paper and write: 'I was ___ centimetres long. Now I am ___ centimetres. I am ___ baby strings long.'

setup.art: A grown-up showing a girl an open child health card with a growth chart and numbers written in pen.
setup.caption: 1. Ask the family, or look at your health card.

setup.art: A short string about 50 centimetres long lying next to a much longer string, on the floor, with labels 'born' and 'now'.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a string as long as you were at birth. Compare.

flow.do: Help your child ask a family member, or look at the child health card together.
flow.say: Let's find out how long and how heavy you were when you were born.
flow.kid: Ask your family. How long were you when you were born? How heavy?
flow.parent: Many Indian families have a Mother and Child Protection card from the anganwadi or hospital, with these numbers. If nobody knows the length, use 50 centimetres, which is close for most babies.

flow.do: Cut a string as long as your child's birth length. Then ask your child to lie down, and lay the string next to them.
flow.say: This string is as long as you were when you were born. Lie down next to it.
flow.kid: Lie down next to the string. That is how long you were.

flow.do: Your child stays lying down. Move the birth-length string along the floor beside them, end to end, from feet to head. Count how many string lengths it takes.
flow.say: How many of these baby strings does it take to make you now?
flow.kid: How many baby strings make you now?

good: More than two.
Two and a bit.

flow.parent: A child of 120 centimetres is a bit more than two 50-centimetre strings.

games.title: Taller, Shorter or Same?
games.context: This is a guessing game about growing. Each card names two people, or one person at two times. Players guess who is usually taller, and show their answer with their hands.

printables.title: 14 cards to cut out, with the answer on the back

items.f: A baby of 1, and a child of 7. Is the child taller, shorter or the same?
items.b: Taller. A child of 7 is often about 45 centimetres taller than a baby of 1.

items.f: A girl of 7, and the same girl at 8. Taller, shorter or the same at 8?
items.b: Taller. Children grow about 5 to 6 centimetres a year.

items.f: A woman of 30, and the same woman at 40. Taller, shorter or the same at 40?
items.b: The same. Adults have stopped getting taller.

items.f: You at bedtime, and you the next morning. Taller, shorter or the same in the morning?
items.b: Taller, a little. The discs in your backbone fill up again at night.

items.f: A newborn baby, and the same baby at 1. Taller, shorter or the same at 1?
items.b: Taller. A baby grows about 25 centimetres in the first year.

items.f: A grandfather at 40, and the same grandfather at 80. Taller, shorter or the same at 80?
items.b: Often a little shorter. Many older people lose a little height.

items.f: A girl of 12, and the same girl at 13. Taller, shorter or the same at 13?
items.b: Taller. Many girls have their growth spurt around this age.

items.f: A man of 20, and the same man at 25. Taller, shorter or the same at 25?
items.b: The same. Most men stop getting taller at about 17 or 18.

items.f: An astronaut on Earth, and the same astronaut in space. Taller, shorter or the same in space?
items.b: Taller, by a few centimetres. Nothing presses the discs in the backbone together in space.

items.f: You in the morning, and you after a long day of play. Taller, shorter or the same after play?
items.b: Shorter, a little. Standing and running press the discs in your backbone.

items.f: A toddler of 2, and the same toddler at 3. Taller, shorter or the same at 3?
items.b: Taller. A toddler grows about 8 centimetres in a year.

items.f: A grown-up's height this year, and next year. Taller, shorter or the same next year?
items.b: The same. Grown-ups do not get taller.

items.f: Two children of 7. One eats well and is healthy. The other is often ill and hungry. After a year, is the child who eats well usually taller, shorter or the same as the other?
items.b: Taller. Food and good health help a body grow.

items.f: A child of 5, and the same child at 10. Taller, shorter or the same at 10?
items.b: Taller. Five years of growing is often about 25 to 30 centimetres.

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
One player reads the front of the top card aloud, and keeps the back hidden.
Everyone shows an answer at the same time: hand held high for taller, hand held low for shorter, hand flat in front for the same.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. Everyone with the right answer gets one point.
Take turns reading. When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Show the three hand signs.
flow.say: Hand up high means taller. Hand down low means shorter. Hand flat means the same.
flow.kid: Hand up means taller. Hand low means shorter. Flat means the same.

flow.do: Take turns reading the cards. Everyone shows a hand sign. Read the back aloud.
flow.say: A woman of 30, and the same woman at 40. Show me! Now let's read the back.
flow.kid: Read a card. Show your hand. Read the back.

good: The astronaut grows in space!
Grown-ups don't get taller.

flow.parent: Let your child explain each answer in their own words before you turn the card.

flow.do: Count the points and talk.
flow.say: Which people on the cards were still growing? Which had stopped?
flow.kid: Count your points. Who was still growing?

check.q: Which of these people is still growing taller?
check.why: Children and teenagers are still growing taller. Adults have stopped, so the woman of 35 and the man of 50 stay the same height.

games.title: Grow to Grown-up: a board game
games.context: This is a race game. Each player starts as a newborn baby and grows along the track to a grown-up. Growing cards tell you when you grow fast and when you grow slowly, as real people do.

printables.title: A track of 20 squares to draw on paper
items: Square 3: 1 year old, 75 cm. Take a card
Square 9: 7 years old, about 120 cm. Take a card

printables.title: 12 growing cards to cut out
items: Babies grow about 25 centimetres in their first year, faster than at any other time. Move 3 squares.
In deep sleep your body makes growth hormone, which helps bones grow. You slept well. Move 1 square.
You ate dal, rice and greens. Your body built new bone. Move 1 square.
You had a fever for a week. Growing slowed down. Miss a turn.
Growth spurt! Many teenagers grow very fast for a year or two. Move 3 squares.
Children lose their first milk tooth at about 6 or 7 years. Move 1 square.
A whole year of slow, steady growing: about 6 centimetres. Move 1 square.
You stood and played all day. The discs in your backbone were squashed a little. Move back 1 square.
You slept all night. The discs in your backbone filled up again. Move 1 square.
You grew out of your school uniform. Move 1 square.
You drank milk and ate ragi. Your body built new bone and muscle. Move 1 square.
A grown-up measured you and drew a new line on the door. Move 1 square.

rules: Each player puts a button or a coin on Start. Put the growing cards face down in a pile.
On your turn, roll a dice and move that many squares. If you have no dice, write 1, 2 and 3 on three small papers, fold them, and pick one each turn.

If you land on square 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18 by moving, take a growing card and do what it says. If a card moves you onto another card square, do not take a second card. You cannot move back past Start.
When the card pile is finished, mix the used cards and make a new pile.
The first player to reach or pass Finish has grown up and wins. The others keep playing until everyone has grown up.

flow.do: Draw the track of 20 squares on paper. Cut out the growing cards and put them face down.
flow.say: This is a life, from a newborn to a grown-up. Let's draw it.
flow.kid: Draw 20 squares. Write Start and Finish. Put the cards in a pile.

flow.do: Play. Read each growing card aloud when someone takes one.
flow.say: You landed on square 6. Take a growing card. What does it say?
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Move. Take a card on squares 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18.

ask.q: Why does the first-year card move you 3 squares?
good: Babies grow very fast in the first year.
A baby grows about 25 centimetres in one year.

flow.parent: Talk about each card as it comes up. The two backbone cards show that height also changes every day.

flow.do: Talk about the game.
flow.say: Which card helped you grow the most? Which slowed you down? Is that true in real life?
flow.kid: Which card helped you grow most?

projects.title: My Growing Chart: measure three times, a month apart
projects.context: In this project you make a height chart on the wall. You measure yourself three times, a month apart, always in the morning. After two months you can see how much you grew.

materials.item: a long strip of chart paper or newspaper, about 1 metre long
cellotape, a hardback book and a pencil
a tailor's tape or a ruler

schedule.what: Tape the chart on the wall. In the morning, measure your height. Draw a line and write the date.
In the morning, measure again. Draw a line, write the date, and measure the gap from last month.
Measure for the third time. Measure how much you grew in two months, and guess how much you will grow in a year.

projects.record: Keep the chart with its three dated lines, and write the three heights in a small table.

setup.art: A long strip of chart paper taped upright on a bedroom wall.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a long paper strip on the wall.

setup.art: Three short pencil lines very close together on the chart, each with a date beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a dated line every month, in the morning.

flow.do: 1. Tape the strip so it does not move. 2. In the morning, measure your child the same way as in the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment: barefoot, against the wall, with a flat book on the head. 3. Draw a line and write the date and the time.
flow.say: We will measure you once a month, always in the morning. Why do we always choose the morning?
flow.kid: Stand straight. Draw your line. Write the date.

ask.q: Why do we always measure in the morning?
good: Because I am taller in the morning, so it must be the same time each month.

flow.do: One month later, measure again in the morning. Measure the gap between the lines in millimetres.
flow.say: One month has gone by. Did you grow? How many millimetres?
flow.kid: Measure again. How many tiny lines between this line and last month's?
flow.parent: In one month most children grow about 4 or 5 millimetres. Some months there may be no change at all.

flow.do: After two months, measure again and work out the growth.
flow.say: In two months, how much did you grow? How much do you think you will grow in a whole year?
flow.kid: How much did you grow in two months?
flow.wait: Two months after the first measuring
flow.parent: Growth of about 1 centimetre in two months is common. A guess for one year of 5 or 6 centimetres is a good answer.

challenges.title: Measure the Wriggler: a fair way to measure someone lying down
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Babies cannot stand, so nurses measure them lying down. Babies also wriggle. Your job is to design a way to measure someone lying down, the same way every time.
challenges.problem: How can you measure a teddy, a doll or a toddler lying down, and get the same answer three times in a row?
constraints: Use only things from home, such as books, a ruler, string, a tray or a steel plate.
The answer must be the same, or within 1 centimetre, three times in a row.
Nothing may press hard on the body being measured.
materials: a soft toy or a doll, or a toddler who agrees to play
two hardback books or two steel plates
a tailor's tape, a ruler or a string
a wall and a flat floor
general: Put the head against a wall, so it always starts at the same place.
Stand a flat book against the soles of the feet, then measure from the wall to the book.
Straighten the legs gently before measuring.
creative: Lay a tailor's tape on a tray, and put a book at each end like a sliding stop.
Draw a line on newspaper at the head and at the feet, then measure between the lines afterwards.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own way. Measure the teddy or doll three times. Did you get the same answer? If not, change your design and try again.

flow.do: Read the challenge with your child.
flow.say: Babies cannot stand up, and they wriggle. How do you think nurses measure them?
flow.kid: Babies cannot stand. How can we measure them lying down?

flow.do: Your child builds a way to measure, and measures the toy three times.
flow.say: Try your idea. Measure three times. Are the answers the same?
flow.kid: Build your measurer. Measure the toy three times.
flow.parent: If a toddler joins in, make it a game and stop if they do not want to. Never press on a child's body.

flow.do: Compare the three answers and improve the design.
flow.say: Were your three answers the same? What made them different?
flow.kid: Were your answers the same? What can you change?

check.q: You measure a doll three times and get 30, 34 and 31 centimetres. What should you do?
options: Find out what changed, and make your way of measuring the same each time
check.why: Different answers mean something changed each time, such as where the head was or how straight the legs were. A good scientist makes the method the same, then measures again.

setup.caption: 1. Head against a wall, a book at the feet.

setup.art: A girl measuring from the wall to the book with a tailor's tape, and writing the number down.

items.p: Put these life stages in order, from youngest to oldest.
items.why: Every person goes through the stages in this order: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult and older adult.
items.art: Six small drawings of people at different ages, mixed up.

items.p: Draw a line from each person to how much they usually grow taller in one year.
pairs: a baby in the first year
items.why: Babies grow fastest. Children grow slowly and steadily. Adults have stopped getting taller.
items.art: A baby, a girl of 7 and a woman, on the left, with three numbers on the right.

items.p: In the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment, you marked your height in blue at bedtime and in red in the morning. Draw the paper strip with both lines.
items.a: A strip with a red line a little above the blue line, with names.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the red morning line a little higher than the blue bedtime line, and says whose lines they are.
items.art: An empty box shaped like a tall paper strip.

items.p: Why were you a little taller in the morning? Say your answer aloud. A grown-up can write it down.
items.a: At night I lay down, and the soft discs in my backbone filled up again.
items.why: A strong answer names the backbone or the discs, and says that lying down takes the weight off them.

items.p: True or false: grown-ups keep getting taller every year.
items.why: False. Most people stop getting taller at about 15 to 18. Some older people even get a little shorter.

items.p: You want to see if you have grown since last month. When should you measure yourself?
opts: At the same time of day as last month
items.why: Height changes during the day. Measuring at the same time each time is fair, so only real growth shows.

items.p: Sort these into things that help a body grow, and things that slow growing down.
items.why: Bones and muscles are built from food. In deep sleep the body makes more growth hormone, which tells bones to grow. Long illness and hunger slow growing down.

items.p: Label the drawing of a backbone: bone, disc.
a: the soft pads between them are discs
items.why: A backbone is a stack of small bones. The soft pads between them are discs.
items.art: A side view of a backbone with two arrows, one to a hard bone and one to a soft pad.

items.p: A newborn baby is about ___ centimetres long.
items.why: Most newborn babies are about 50 centimetres long, a little less than two 30-centimetre school rulers laid end to end.

items.p: Draw yourself in clothes from three years ago. Show with arrows where they are too small.
items.a: A drawing with arrows at the wrists, knees or waist.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the sleeves or the length too short, because arms and legs grow a lot in childhood.

items.p: A child drew round the feet of everyone at home. The grandmother's foot was smaller than the mother's, though the grandmother is older. Why might that be? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: Grown-ups stop growing. The grandmother's feet stopped growing long ago, and grown-ups' sizes are all different.
items.why: A strong answer says that adults have stopped growing, so age does not set foot size after the teens.

items.p: Why do doctors write the time of day next to a child's height?
opts: Height changes a little during the day
Children grow only at some hours
items.why: Height changes a little between morning and evening. With the time written down, two measurements can be compared fairly.

items.p: Kavya, Amma and Ajji did the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment. Everyone was a little taller in the morning. Now they are talking about which height is the real one.

views.says: Our real height is the morning one, because that is when our backbone is not squashed.
Our real height is the evening one, because that is how tall we are most of the day.
Both are real. Height changes in a day, so we should always write down the time.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right. A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and gives a reason. Kavya is right that the morning is the most stretched height. Amma is right that we spend most of the day shorter. Ajji is right that both are measurements of real heights.
items.why: There is no single true height. A fair answer uses the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment and says why writing the time matters.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest to the tallest.
items.why: A newborn is about 50 centimetres, a toddler about 85, a girl of 7 about 120, and a woman about 150 to 160.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? A girl of 8, a boy of 12, a woman of 50, a toddler of 3.
items.why: The woman of 50 has stopped getting taller. The other three are still growing.

items.p: Draw two backbones: one in the evening, after a long day, and one in the morning, after sleep.
items.a: Evening: thin, flat discs. Morning: thicker, rounder discs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same bones, with thinner discs in the evening and thicker discs in the morning.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'evening' and 'morning'.

items.p: True or false: astronauts get a little taller in space.
items.why: True. In space nothing presses the discs of the backbone together, so astronauts get a few centimetres taller. They shrink back on Earth.

items.p: A child grows about 6 centimetres in a year. In two years, that child grows about ___ centimetres.
items.why: 6 centimetres and 6 centimetres make 12 centimetres.

items.p: A boy of 3 wants to be measured standing on tiptoes. Why is that not fair? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: Tiptoes make him look taller than he is. Every measurement must be done the same way, heels down.
items.why: A strong answer says the method must be the same each time, so only real growing shows.

items.p: A girl of 7 grows 5 millimetres in a month. Why can she not see herself growing?
opts: It is far too slow to notice
She is not growing at all
items.why: 5 millimetres a month is only about a millimetre a week. That is too slow to see, so we draw lines and measure.

items.p: A doctor measures a girl of 8 at 9 in the morning. Next month a different doctor measures her at 6 in the evening. She seems to have grown nothing. Has she really stopped growing? Explain. A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: Maybe not. She was measured in the evening, when people are a little shorter. Her growth may be hidden by the time of day.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment: people are a little shorter in the evening, so a morning height and an evening height are not fair to compare.

items.p: Two scientists are arguing about how babies grow.

views.who: Michelle Lampl, who measured babies very often
views.says: Babies grow in sudden jumps, with days or weeks of no growing in between.
Small mistakes in measuring a wriggling baby make smooth growing look like jumps.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What could you do to find out? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: A strong answer picks one side, then suggests a test: measure a baby very carefully, many times, in the same way each day, and see whether the jumps stay.
items.why: This is still argued about. A good answer suggests careful, repeated measuring, like the Measure the Wriggler challenge.

items.p: In the WHO growth study, well-fed, healthy babies in India, Ghana, Brazil and Norway were measured. What did the scientists find?
opts: Indian babies always grew much less
Norwegian babies always grew much less
items.why: Healthy babies with good food and care grew almost the same in all six countries. So food and health matter a lot.

items.p: Draw a picture graph of how tall a person is at 0, 1, 7, 15 and 30 years old.
items.a: Five people getting taller quickly at first, then more slowly, with the 15-year-old and 30-year-old close in height.
items.why: A strong graph shows fast growing as a baby, steady growing in childhood, and no growing after the teens.
items.art: An empty grid with ages 0, 1, 7, 15 and 30 along the bottom.

items.p: A girl of 7 grew 6 centimetres last year. Her mother grew nothing. Both ate the same food. Why the difference? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: Her mother is an adult. The growing parts of her bones turned to hard bone in her teens, so she cannot get taller.
items.why: A strong answer says adults have stopped growing taller, whatever they eat.

items.p: True or false: a person grows at exactly the same speed every year of their life.
items.why: False. Babies grow fastest, children grow slowly and steadily, teenagers have a growth spurt, and adults do not grow taller.

items.p: Draw a line from each one to the way of measuring that fits.
pairs: standing against a wall with a flat book on the head
dated pencil lines on a door frame
items.why: Babies cannot stand, so they are measured lying down. Children stand. Dated lines let a family see growth over the years.

items.p: Look at the growth chart and label the parts: baby grows fast, child grows steadily, teen growth spurt, grown-up stops.
items.why: A height chart rises steeply in the first year, gently through childhood, steeply again in the teens, and then goes flat.
items.art: A curved line rising steeply at first, then gently, then steeply again, then flat, with four empty label boxes.

items.p: Sort these changes into two groups: changes that happen to children as they grow, and changes that happen to many older adults.
items.why: Children lose milk teeth and their feet grow. Many older adults get grey hair and lose a little height.

items.p: Why do health workers measure a baby lying down, but a child of 7 standing up? A grown-up can write down what you say.
items.a: A baby cannot stand still, so lying down is the way to measure the same each time. A child can stand straight against a wall.
items.why: A strong answer says the method must suit the body and be the same each time.

quiz.p: Which life stage comes right after toddler?
quiz.why: The stages go baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult, older adult.

quiz.p: When do people grow fastest after they are born?
quiz.why: A baby grows about 25 centimetres in the first year. That is the fastest growing after birth.

quiz.p: About how much does a child of 7 grow in one year?
quiz.why: Children grow slowly and steadily, about 5 or 6 centimetres a year. 50 centimetres is the length of a newborn.

quiz.p: When are most people a little taller?
opts: In the evening, after a busy day

quiz.p: What are the soft pads between the bones of your backbone called?

quiz.p: You measure yourself every month. What makes your measuring fair?

opts: One try can be a little wrong

quiz.why: 8 take away 5 is 3. The first child's height changed 3 millimetres more than the other child's.

open_questions.q: Do children grow a tiny bit every day, or in sudden jumps?
open_questions.why_open: Michelle Lampl found jumps when she measured babies very often. Other scientists think measuring mistakes may cause some of the jumps. It is still argued about.

open_questions.q: What tells the growing parts of bones when to stop?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know chemical messages in the body play a part, but they do not fully understand how bones know when the body is grown up.

open_questions.q: Why do humans have such a long childhood?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists say it gives time to learn. Others say a big brain takes a long time to grow. Many think both matter, but nobody knows for sure.

maths.problem: A girl of 7 and her mother did the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment. The girl's red morning line was 6 millimetres above her blue bedtime line. Her mother's was 12 millimetres above. How many times bigger was her mother's change?
maths.explain: 6 and 6 make 12. So her mother's change was two lots of the girl's change.
maths.context: This is about the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment, where you marked your height at bedtime and again in the morning.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two changes shows who changed more, and how much more, not just that both changed.

maths.problem: A newborn baby is 50 centimetres long. After one year, the baby is 75 centimetres. How much did the baby grow?
maths.explain: Count on from 50 to 75: that is 25. That is about four or five times what a child of 7 grows in a year.
maths.context: This is about the card on how fast children grow.
maths.why_maths: Taking away the first length from the second shows how much growing happened.

maths.problem: A child grows about 6 centimetres a year. The child is 130 centimetres tall now. About how tall will the child be in two years?
maths.explain: 6 and 6 make 12. 130 and 12 make 142. This is only a guess, because children do not grow exactly the same every year.
maths.context: This is about the My Growing Chart project, where you measure yourself once a month.
maths.why_maths: Adding the growth for each year lets you predict, and later check your prediction.

maths.problem: You measure your height three times and get 121 centimetres, 122 centimetres and 121 centimetres. Which number should you write down, and why?
maths.explain: Two of the three tries say 121. When you put the three numbers in order, the middle one is also 121. The try that gave 122 was a little off.
maths.context: This is about why we measure three times in the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment.
maths.why_maths: Looking at all three numbers together shows which one is the real height and which was a small mistake.

roots.context: We have learnt how a body grows from a baby to a grown-up, and how to measure growing carefully. Now we ask what the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment tells us about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment, you marked your height at bedtime, and next morning the mark was a little higher. You did not grow that much in one night. The discs in your backbone are pressed thin during the day and fill up again when you lie down. So a body's size goes up and down every day, as well as growing over the years.
deep_truth.habit: We think of our height as one fixed number about us, like our name. But a body is always changing, even in a single day. Every measurement is a measurement at one time.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Bedtime Tall, Morning Tall experiment, the red morning lines were higher than the blue bedtime lines, usually by a few millimetres for a child and more for a grown-up. A doctor in England wrote about the same change 300 years ago. Studies of children since then find a daily change of about half a centimetre to one and a half centimetres.

three.who_am_i: You are a body that keeps changing: bigger every year, taller every morning, a little shorter every evening. And you are still you.
three.what_is_life: A living body keeps building itself, again and again. It builds with food and sleep, and it needs the care of other people.
three.what_is_this_world: Everything that lives is growing or changing all the time, even when it is too slow to see: a mango tree, a calf, a grandmother, you.

roots.thread: You began very small, and every part of you since then has been built from food: milk, rice, dal, greens. The food came from plants, and the plants grew from sunlight, water and soil. So the water and soil of a paddy field in Thanjavur can become part of your thigh bone. Your body is always taking in new material and changing.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that a person passes through childhood, youth and old age in the same body. A wise person is not confused by these changes.
teachings.link: In this unit, a body changes from baby to child to adult, and even from night to morning. Yet the person inside feels like the same person.

other_view.view: The Buddha taught anatta: there is no fixed self that stays the same through all the changes. In this view, there is only a stream of changes, and the 'same me' is a habit of thinking.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many doctors thought children in different countries naturally grow to different sizes. If babies in India were smaller than babies in the United States, people said that was just how Indian babies are. So nobody could tell whether a small child was healthy or not getting enough food. In 1997, the World Health Organization began a big study, led by Dr Mercedes de Onis. Scientists followed healthy babies in six countries: Brazil, Ghana, India, Norway, Oman and the United States. The babies were breastfed and had good food and care. In India, the work was done in South Delhi by a team that included Dr Nita Bhandari. The babies were measured again and again in their first two years. The result surprised many people. Babies in all six countries grew almost the same. So when many children in one place grow less, the main reason is usually food, illness and dirty water, not the country they live in. In 2006 the WHO made new growth charts from this study. Anganwadis and doctors in India use these charts today.
how_we_found_out.who: Dr Mercedes de Onis at the World Health Organization, and teams in six countries, including Dr Nita Bhandari and her colleagues in New Delhi
how_we_found_out.when: The study ran from 1997 to 2003. The new growth charts came out in 2006.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That children in poorer countries are naturally smaller, so being small is normal for them. Measuring healthy, well-fed babies in six countries showed they all grow almost the same.
